sentences.text: Welcome to the pulsars tour.
It all began in 1967, when Jocelyn Bell, a PhD student at Cambridge, noticed a strange signal in the radio data that repeated every 1. 3 seconds.
The signal was so regular that her team half-jokingly named it LGM 1, meaning Little Green Men.
PSR B 1919 plus 21, before you, is that very first pulsar.
It was in fact a neutron star, spinning like a lighthouse and directing its beam toward us on every turn.
The Crab Pulsar is the neutron star left behind by the supernova of 1054.
It spins 30 times a second and lights up the entire Crab Nebula with its energy.
It is only 20 kilometers across, yet heavier than the Sun; a sugar-cube-sized piece of its matter weighs as much as a mountain.
It pulses at every wavelength, from radio waves to gamma rays.
It is the first pulsar definitively matched to an observable supernova, and it proved that pulsars are born from exploding stars.
The Hulse–Taylor binary was the setting for one of the most important experiments in physics.
In this system, discovered in 1974, a pulsar and another neutron star orbit their common center of mass once every 7 hours and 45 minutes.
Their orbits shrink by a few millimeters every year.
This matches exactly the energy loss through gravitational waves that Einstein predicted: the first indirect evidence for general relativity.
With this discovery, Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1993.
The two stars will merge within 300 million years.
PSR J 1748 minus 2446 A D is the fastest-spinning pulsar known: 716 revolutions a second.
The speed at its equator approaches a quarter of the speed of light; if it spun even a little faster, it would fly apart.
It reached this speed by accelerating for millions of years on matter drawn from its companion star.
It lives in a dense globular cluster called Terzan 5, in the constellation Sagittarius.
Its companion is swollen by the pulsar's intense radiation, and for about 40 percent of the orbit it covers the pulsar and cuts off its signal.
The first exoplanets were found not around a Sun-like star, but around a dead star.
In 1992, Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail deduced the planets orbiting this pulsar, named Lich, from millisecond delays in its pulse.
These three planets, named Draugr, Poltergeist, and Phobetor, probably re-formed from debris left over from the supernova.
Draugr is the least massive exoplanet known; it weighs only twice as much as the Moon.
Under the pulsar's lethal radiation, life cannot even be imagined; that is why their names are taken from ghosts and the living dead.
Our final stop is a magnetar: SGR 1806 minus 20.
Magnetars are neutron stars with the strongest magnetic fields in the universe; this field is a thousand trillion times stronger than Earth's, and from 1,000 kilometers away it erases a credit card.
On December 27, 2004, its crust cracked and, in a tenth of a second, it flung out as much energy as the Sun emits in 100,000 years.
This explosion, coming from 50,000 light-years away, measurably ionized Earth's upper atmosphere and blinded the detectors of satellites.
It is the brightest event observed from outside the Solar System to date.
Our pulsars tour has come to an end.
The Vela Pulsar is one of the brightest radio pulsars, 1,000 light-years away.
It is the remnant of a star that exploded 11,000 years ago, and it spins 11 times a second.
From time to time it suddenly speeds up; these events are called glitches.
They are the result of quakes in the star's solid crust, or of the superfluid neutrons in its interior transferring energy to the crust.
So by studying this little star, we learn how matter behaves at densities that cannot be produced in any laboratory on Earth.
